title: Why gates sag: post, brace, cable

A.name: IMG_2819.jpg
A.note: band aligned to the right edge so the AC unit (and the left post) are out of frame; the right post carries the right leaf's hinges (checked at 3x), so it is the ringed hinge post

headline: GATE *SAGGING?*
CHECK THE *POST*
beats.vo: Gate sagging? Most sagging gates start at the post.

headline: HINGE POST =
*STRONGEST*
beats.vo: The *hinge post* carries the gate like a lever. Make it the *strongest* post you have, set in concrete.

headline: LOW HINGE TO
*HIGH LATCH*
beats.vo: Wood gate brace? *Bottom hinge corner* up to *top latch corner*. Backwards, it sags.

headline: A CABLE GOES
THE *OTHER WAY*
beats.vo: An *anti-sag cable* runs the opposite way, and the *turnbuckle* lifts the latch side.

headline: WELDED FRAMES
*STAY SQUARE*
beats.vo: Welded metal frames *stay square* longer, but they still need a solid post.
Does your gate sag? Comment below.

post.caption: Why gates sag around the Lower Mainland: it usually starts at the hinge post, so make that the strongest post on the run. On a wood gate the brace runs from the bottom hinge corner up to the top latch corner; an anti-sag cable runs the opposite way.
post.alt: A wide cedar gate on heavy posts, an animated diagram showing the correct diagonal brace and anti-sag cable directions, and a black metal gate with a welded frame.
